title: Wailing on the Housetops
english: … “the axe lies at the root of the trees; every tree, then, that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matthew 3:10).

Since Israel, then, gave free rein to its advance in sin, and was devoted, as I said just now, to the false worship of idols, God through the prophet foretells the capture of Jerusalem that would come in its time, and says: “What has happened to you now, that you have all gone up to useless housetops? The city is filled with people shouting. Your wounded are not wounded by the sword, nor are your dead the dead of war” (Isaiah 22:1–2).

It seems to point here to the devastation in the days of Jeconiah, and to accuse those of Israel severely, because even amid these very evils, in misfortunes at their very height, they did not know how to do what leads to their good and what would win them favor from above. For they ought to have gone up to the house of God weeping and lamenting, to promise repentance, to ask pardon for the outrages they had committed, and to seek the helping hand from him, and from him alone.

And he himself taught this, saying through one of the holy prophets: “Gird yourselves and beat your breasts, you priests; wail, you who minister at the altar. Go in, sleep in sackcloth, you who minister to God, for sacrifice and drink offering are withheld from your house. Sanctify a fast, proclaim a solemn service, gather the elders, all who dwell in the land, into the house of your God, and cry out earnestly to the Lord: Alas, alas, for the day” (Joel 1:13–15).

These are the things they ought to have done to appease the one who has power to save, since he had been provoked. But it seems that they did not even let it enter their minds that they ought to do these things. Instead they went up to the highest parts of their houses, and everywhere there were laments, and the wailing of children, wasting away, it may be, from hunger and thirst. For such things must happen to cities under siege.

That is why he says: “What has happened to you now, that you have all gone up to useless housetops?” Why, he says, even amid terrors so unbearable, when your peril had reached its last extremity and everything was at stake, did you not cry out to God, but instead leapt up to the housetops, though that did you no good at all? That is why he calls them useless housetops.

And why was the city filled with people shouting? Not, surely, people crying to God, but people crying out at random, and all but beside themselves at the evils that had come within their doors. The lament ought to have been for repentance; the tears ought to have been shed before God. title: How Tyre Fell
english: … to wall them in, to keep them beyond the reach of any attack, and to show them stronger than the Babylonians.

In another way, too, they themselves joined in plundering the nation of the Jews: on the one hand by falling on them when they were worn down and seizing those who were left; on the other by dedicating sacred vessels to their falsely named gods, and by driving those who had come under the yoke of slavery to them away, by force as it were, from the worship the law prescribes. And so God said through one of the holy prophets: “And what are you to me, Tyre and Sidon and all Galilee of the foreigners? Are you paying me back, or do you bear a grudge against me? Swiftly and speedily I will return your payment on your own heads, because you took my silver and my gold, and carried my choice and fine things into your temples, and you sold the sons of Judah and the sons of Israel to the sons of the Greeks, to drive them out of their own borders” (Joel 3:4–6).

So Tyre too was captured through the wrath of God, in this way. It was an island, with a strait still running between, which separated it from the mainland by no great distance. When the Babylonian came and sought to take it along with the other cities, he ordered the armies under his command to fill in the sea between, to join it to the mainland, and to let it remain an island no longer. When this had been done, or was expected to be done before long, most of those in Tyre, since trade was their occupation and they were used to sailing, sailed away from the island with their children and wives and went off to other cities and villages.

The Babylonians then marched in, killed those who remained, took many captive, and did what victors usually do. Yet they were grieved not a little to learn that a great many, among them the most prominent in the city, had put their goods on ships and fled.

The prophecy of Ezekiel also records this history. For the God of all spoke to him thus: “Son of man, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon made his army serve a great service against Tyre; every head was made bald, and every shoulder rubbed bare, yet neither he nor his army received any wages for the hard service he served against Tyre. In return for this I have given him the land of Egypt” (Ezekiel 29:18–20). For after the capture of the Tyrians the Babylonian turned the war against the nation of the Egyptians.

title: Why the Earth Is Cursed
english: … of the glory of the children of God (compare Romans 8:21).
“Because they transgressed the law and changed the ordinances, an everlasting covenant, therefore a curse will devour the earth, because those who dwell in it have sinned” (Isaiah 24:5–6).

The discourse returns again to the exact sense of the prophecy. So that no one may think that the God of all brings punishments on anyone without cause, the prophets join the causes to the stirrings of wrath and plainly announce the charges against those who are punished. The earth will mourn, then; for what cause? “Because they transgressed the law and broke the everlasting covenant.” That is why he says: “And the earth will be accursed, for those who dwell in it have done wrong.”

Since the land of the Jews too, together with the other cities or countries, was made to pay the penalty (for it was laid waste, as I said), the prophet again seems to bring into the open the offenses of those under the law. “For they transgressed the law,” he says. Those of Israel held it of no account, and turned as it were onto another path, giving heed to teachings that are commandments of men (compare Isaiah 29:13).

Taking the words in their universal sense and giving their meaning, we say that in the beginning the God of all fashioned man and engraved on him a natural law, training him toward the knowledge of evil and good. And this, I think, is what was said through the voice of John about the only-begotten Son of God: “He was the true light, which enlightens every man coming into the world” (John 1:9). We understand that this also came about in the last times, I mean the times of his coming. For it is written: “In those days, says the Lord, putting my laws into their mind, I will also write them on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33; Hebrews 8:10).

This law, then, which steers us from within toward the knowledge of good and evil, those on the earth transgressed, and they changed the ordinances. For though they were created for good works (compare Ephesians 2:10), they turned to love of the flesh and to an earthly mind. That is why the earth has become accursed: those who dwell in it have offended the Creator by a great many wrongs.

“Therefore those who dwell in the earth will be poor, and few people will be left” (Isaiah 24:6). For since, he says, the earth has become accursed because so very much lawlessness arose in it, they will therefore be weighed down by unexpected poverty and will barely be saved; for those left will be few and easily counted.
